content.p: The Rock Machine began as a Montreal outlaw motorcycle club and became known for one thing: it was the smaller side in the longest and deadliest biker conflict in Canadian history. Between 1994 and 2002 its members, allies and enemies fought the Hells Angels for the Quebec drug trade. The Canadian Encyclopedia counts more than 160 dead and more than 200 wounded, with bombings, arson and disappearances on top, and many of the casualties were bystanders.

The club did not win. By the end of 2000 it was being picked apart by defections, and it was absorbed into the American-based Bandidos, who in turn were swept up by police and left Quebec to the Hells Angels. The name did not die, though. A club called the Rock Machine turned up in Winnipeg about a decade later, and police there described a new turf fight with Hells Angels affiliates.
content.h2: Two old friends and a massacre
content.p: The story begins with two men who had once run the same gang. According to The Canadian Encyclopedia, Salvatore Cazzetta and Maurice Boucher led a white-supremacist motorcycle club called the SS in the early 1980s, which dominated organized crime in Pointe-aux-Trembles in Montreal. They fell out after Boucher joined the Hells Angels. Cazzetta, the Encyclopedia says, regarded any link with the Angels as unforgivable after the Lennoxville killings of 24 March 1985, when the Angels executed five of their own members at a clubhouse in Sherbrooke to settle a dispute between two Quebec chapters.

In response, the Encyclopedia says, Cazzetta formed his own club, the Rock Machine, with his brother Giovanni. The pair, it says, were the dominant organized-crime figures in every part of Montreal that the Mafia did not control. The Encyclopedia adds that the Hells Angels were tied to the Mafia, while the brothers had ties to other syndicates, especially francophone ones. Both sides built "puppet clubs", small affiliated clubs that supply recruits and insulate full members from criminal exposure.
content.h2: An ultimatum and a first killing
content.p: In 1994 the balance shifted. Salvatore Cazzetta received a 10-year sentence in Florida for attempting to smuggle cocaine, the Encyclopedia reports; he was moved to a Quebec prison in 2002 and paroled in 2004. With him gone, the Encyclopedia says, Boucher had the opening he had been waiting for. The Encyclopedia and the Montreal Gazette both describe an ultimatum issued by the Hells Angels: with very few exceptions, anyone dealing drugs in Montreal had to buy from them. The Encyclopedia put the market at about $1 billion a year.

Opponents of the ultimatum, among them Giovanni Cazzetta, organized an alliance. The Gazette says its leaders met weeks before the first killing and called the group "the Alliance"; the Encyclopedia calls it the Alliance Against the Angels, also known as the Dark Circle; the Gazette names the Rock Machine as one of its dominant groups.

On 13 July 1994 three masked men walked into a custom motorcycle shop in the Rivière-des-Prairies district. The Gazette reports that they called out to the owner twice to be sure of their target and then fired at least 16 bullets. The victim, Pierre Daoust, 34, belonged to the Death Riders, a club that supported the Hells Angels, and was declared dead hours later. The killing drew little press attention, the Gazette notes, but drug dealers across Montreal understood it. The next day someone tried to kill Normand Robitaille, a member of another Angels support club, who survived. The Gazette adds that police announced the arrest of five Rock Machine members over a plot to blow up the South Shore clubhouse of an Angels support club, the Evil Ones.

A former Angel who became an informant, Sylvain Boulanger, told police that all four Quebec Angels chapters voted unanimously by the end of August 1994 to join the war, the Gazette reports. That vote, in the Gazette's account, left the Montreal Angels with far more backing than the Alliance.
content.h2: Bombs, a boy and a federal law
content.p: For a year the conflict produced shootings, bombings and killings on both sides. On 9 August 1995 a car bomb exploded in Hochelaga-Maisonneuve, in east Montreal. The Encyclopedia says the driver, drug dealer Marc Dubé, was killed and 11-year-old Daniel Desrochers, who had been playing on the street, was hit in the head by shrapnel and died in hospital five days later. The Globe and Mail says the outrage that followed led to Bill C-95, which stiffened penalties for offenders shown to belong to established criminal organizations. The Encyclopedia ties both Bill C-95 (1997) and Bill C-24 (2001) to the case, and says Desrochers' death led to the launch of Operation Carcajou on 5 October 1995, a joint task force of the RCMP, the Sûreté du Québec and Montreal police, which it says achieved little amid political infighting.

The largest mass killing of the war came in September 1995, according to the Globe and Mail. Rock Machine members tried to plant a bomb at the clubhouse of an Angels-affiliated gang, were spotted, and the device exploded and killed three of their own supporters. The Encyclopedia lists a crowded week that month with an assassination in a parking lot, bombings and arson attacks on businesses, and says by January 1996 the war had caused 28 deaths in 18 months.

The Globe and Mail judged that when the turf war peaked in the mid-1990s the Hells Angels were winning, with greater resources, and were systematically eliminating their rivals. Other incidents sat outside the club-versus-club frame. In a 1999 robbery described to a Montreal court, four Rock Machine gunmen robbed a trucker of marijuana that belonged to a runner for an Angels affiliate, the Jokers; the Globe reports that the runner, Gaétan Michelin, was found shot dead the next evening. The Angels, it says, concluded the theft was an inside job.
content.h2: The late 1990s and the turn of the century
content.p: The Encyclopedia describes two of the most shocking crimes of the war, the 1997 murders of prison guards Diane Lavigne and Pierre Rondeau. It says they were ordered by Boucher and carried out by a biker who wanted to enter the Angels' Nomads unit. Boucher was found guilty in May 2002 of attempted murder and two first-degree murder counts for ordering the attacks on the three prison guards and sentenced to life with no chance of parole for 25 years, the Encyclopedia says; he died in prison on 10 July 2022.

In 2000 the killings accelerated. The Globe and Mail wrote in July of that year that the war had cost about 150 lives since 1994, with a dozen further disappearances and at least 159 attempted homicides, and that the year might prove the bloodiest yet. It described the shooting of loan shark Bob Savard, a confidant of Boucher, in a north Montreal restaurant, where 15 patrons dived under their tables and a waitress was wounded. Gerald Gallant, a hit man turned informant who received 48 life sentences in 2008, confessed that he carried out that killing, according to the Toronto Sun. The Sun describes the Rock Machine as allies of Gallant's boss, Raymond Desfosses.

The shooting of crime reporter Michel Auger in September 2000, six shots in the back in the parking lot of the Journal de Montréal, brought public fury, the Encyclopedia says. Auger survived and was back at work within three months. The Encyclopedia says the Angels had taken a contract out on him. It says the Hells Angels and the Rock Machine then announced a ceasefire, brokered through the Rizzuto crime family between Boucher and the Rock Machine's president, Frédéric Faucher, and that it lasted only a few weeks. The Gazette frames the truce differently, as an Angels offer to the Quebec Bandidos with a hidden agenda: to stop the Bandidos growing in Canada and to peel away members.

Sources do not agree on the date the Rock Machine became Bandidos. The Encyclopedia says the club became allies of the Bandidos in 1999. The Gazette says that in summer 1999 it became a probationary Bandidos club and that the remaining members officially joined the Bandidos on 6 January 2001 at a party in Kingston, Ontario. The Globe and Mail reported in December 2000 that the alliance was made official in early December and in February 2001 that the Bandidos established probationary chapters that December after "taking over" the Rock Machine.

What is clear from the Globe and Mail is that the move was followed almost at once by defections. Paul "Sasquatch" Porter, a Rock Machine founder whom the Globe called its highest-profile player in Ontario, switched to the Hells Angels in the last weeks of 2000. In a message on the club's website as it took its new colours, he wrote "Bye my brothers". The Globe counted him as one of at least 11 supporters who had jumped, and quoted a police officer saying the gangs were fighting a "corporate war". Rock Machine members posted bitter replies naming the dead. In June 2005 the Globe wrote that Porter and another former Rock Machine soldier, Brett Simmons, had formally joined the Hells Angels in December 2000.

In February 2001 the new Bandidos in Quebec were hit again. Alain Brunet, president of the Kingston probationary chapter, was wounded in an ambush on a highway north of Montreal, and the next day Michel Gauthier, a "hang-around" of a probationary Bandidos club, was found shot dead, the Globe reported. A police officer told the paper: "All the main leaders of the Rock Machine are now either dead, in jail or joined the Hells Angels."

The CBC covered a related legal test in January 2001. Eight alleged Rock Machine members in Verdun, including Francois Laporte, Daniel Leclerc and Mario Filion, were charged under the new anti-gang law, which made membership in a criminal organization an aggravating factor. Their lawyer argued the Verdun group had ceased to exist. The Crown's star witness, informant Peter Paradis, said that after the murder of Rock Machine leader Renaud Jomphe the group fell into a "me, myself and I" attitude. The CBC page does not give the verdict.

On 28 March 2001 police launched Operation Springtime, a coordinated raid involving the RCMP, the Sûreté du Québec, the Ontario Provincial Police, Montreal police and 23 other municipal forces, according to the Encyclopedia. It says hundreds of bikers across Canada were arrested, among them Boucher and 41 associates; the Gazette also records drug trafficking and murder-conspiracy charges. A later Globe report says more than 120 bikers were arrested and quoted former Quebec police biker expert Guy Ouellette saying that only 59 Hells Angels remained free in Quebec afterwards.

The Gazette says the arrests opened a drug-trafficking gap that the surviving Bandidos tried to fill, but an investigation begun in April 2000 grew into Operation Amigo. On 5 June 2002 charges were filed against 62 people tied to the Bandidos, the Gazette says. The Globe reports that about 300 officers raided homes and clubhouses in Toronto, Kingston, Montreal and Quebec City and arrested 26 members, and the Gazette adds that the sweep removed the Bandidos' entire Montreal membership. For the first time since 1994 one side of the conflict was behind bars, and the Gazette said that ended the war. The Encyclopedia adds that the Bandidos ceded Quebec to the Hells Angels in 2003, and credits the war's end to police pressure, exhaustion and defections.

By 2006 the Globe and Mail described the Bandidos as a minor presence in Canada. Years later a club using the Rock Machine name surfaced in Manitoba. Whether it has any organizational link to the Montreal club is not established on the pages consulted, and the news reports on it do not say.

In July 2011 Winnipeg police told Global News about seven attempted firebombings and five shot-up homes and businesses in a few weeks, and said a 14-year-old had been hurt; the conflict was "said to involve affiliates of the Rock Machine and the Hells Angels". A police affidavit cited by CBC in April 2012 counted 20 reported incidents between the Hells Angels puppet group Redlined Support Crew and the Rock Machine the previous summer, most of them unsolved, and sought peace bonds against nine men. Gangsters Inc., relying on Winnipeg Free Press coverage of court records, reported that police counted more than 50 violent acts since the Rock Machine came onto their radar in January 2010. A Winnipeg detective in those records said that street sources believed the Rock Machine wanted to take over the Angels' market. In October 2012 a Rock Machine sergeant-at-arms, Jean Paul Beaumont, was found stabbed to death in a Brandon jail cell, the Brandon Sun reported; the death was classed as suspicious.

According to the Encyclopedia, Salvatore Cazzetta joined the Hells Angels after his release in 2005 and was alleged to have led their Quebec chapter from 2011 to 2015. He was arrested in 2009 and again in November 2015. Charges of gangsterism and conspiracy to commit fraud were dropped in 2017 by a Quebec Superior Court judge because of delay in bringing the case to trial, although he was refused bail on other counts, including conspiracy to traffic narcotics. In 2018 he sued the Attorney General of Quebec for $2 million over detention between November 2015 and August 2017. Those allegations were not proven in court on the pages consulted.
